Two new Apple Watch features may violate privacy laws in multiple US states, as the new “Live Listen” and “Siri Conversation Summary” features record conversations.

The devil is in the details—both features do not allow anyone to access the recordings, and it seems court testing will be needed to establish new legal precedent……

Live Listen and Siri Conversation Summary

Apple announced that the latest Apple Watch models support four audio intelligence features that use the built-in microphone:

  • Sound recognition, which can identify sounds like doorbells and fire alarms
  • Music recognition, powered by Shazam technology
  • Live Listen, which can convert a conversation you just missed into text
  • Siri Conversation Summary, which provides a high-level summary of a conversation

It is precisely the latter two features that have sparked privacy controversy, because they record everything you and everyone around you say.

Recording laws

The legality of recording and when it applies varies by state or country.

Many US states have adopted the so-called “two-party consent” rule, meaning all parties in a conversation must know about and consent to being recorded. In these states, using any device to record a conversation without the other party’s knowledge or consent is illegal. (Law enforcement has specific exceptions, but those are not relevant to this discussion.)

If the Apple Watch truly stores recordings and can play them back, the laws in these states are clear: consent must be obtained first. The complication is that Apple has explicitly stated that this is not the case.

Apple’s privacy measures

Apple has clearly put considerable effort into privacy, and we have previously discussed how they introduce each feature.

Neither feature runs in the background by default—each must be manually activated every time. Live Listen must be reactivated each time it is used and only runs for 15 seconds. The recordings cannot be accessed by anyone and are stored only on a separate encrypted chip.

Recordings are stored only briefly, used to generate transcripts or summaries, and then deleted immediately.

Legal uncertainty

Despite the above measures, Bloomberg cited legal experts pointing out that these new features create legal uncertainty.

Bloomberg reporter Natalie Lung interviewed lawyers in California, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, and Washington on September 11. These states generally prohibit wiretapping private or confidential conversations without the consent of all participants……Without exception, the lawyers she interviewed believed Apple’s safeguards were insufficient to provide the wearer with adequate legal liability protection……Even if the conversation is only continuously processed and ultimately does not produce a recording in the traditional sense, it may still be considered wiretapping under state law. Pennsylvania defense attorney Phil Lauer said the technology is “close to legal because no one actually receives and uses the data.” But he added that it “could still be considered illegal” because the device is collecting and analysing audio. Lauer noted: “Given the various privacy protections Apple has implemented, whether the courts will take the same view is an interesting question, and one that is about to arise.”

9to5Mac’s view

This is yet another example of the law failing to keep up with technology. If recordings are only used to generate transcripts or summaries, but no one can directly access them, does that count as violating anti-recording laws? The short answer seems to be: no one knows.

Live Listen in particular looks harmless. It only records the last 15 seconds of a conversation, and emits a tone each time it is activated, even if the watch is in silent mode or connected to headphones.

Ultimately this question will likely need to be tested in court. The dilemma facing Apple Watch wearers is: if the court rules that the new features fall within the scope of the relevant laws, the legal liability rests on the wearer, not Apple.
